analysis.one_liner: Exempts 95% of foreign profits U.S. multinational companies bring home from federal tax.
analysis.headline: Senator Enzi's bill to exempt most foreign corporate profits from U.S. tax drew zero cosponsors and never received a committee vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would move the U.S. from taxing American companies' worldwide profits toward a 'territorial' system: dividends a U.S. company receives from its foreign subsidiaries would be 95% tax-free, income from U.S.-developed intangibles like patents used abroad would get a 50% deduction, and companies could elect to bring home profits already parked overseas at roughly 30% of the normal tax rate, payable in up to eight installments. It pairs these tax cuts with some anti-avoidance rules, including a new tax on foreign income taxed abroad at less than half the U.S. corporate rate and a crackdown on interest-deduction shifting. It was referred to the Finance Committee on the day it was introduced and received no further action, no cosponsors, and no vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: U.S. multinational corporations with large foreign operations and profits. Their dividends from foreign subsidiaries would be almost entirely tax-free; profits from U.S.-developed patents, software, and other intangibles used abroad would get a 50% deduction; and companies electing the transition rule could bring accumulated offshore profits home while paying tax on only 30% of them, spread over up to eight years.

how_it_helps.text: Allows a 95% deduction for the foreign-source portion of dividends domestic corporations receive from their controlled foreign corporations, so only 5% of such dividends remain taxable.

Lets U.S. companies treat gain on the sale of foreign corporation stock held at least one year as a dividend eligible for the 95% deduction, and adds a 50% deduction for foreign intangible income derived from intangible property developed or substantially enhanced in the United States.

Lets a U.S. shareholder elect a 70% deduction on certain amounts from controlled foreign corporations — including accumulated pre-2013 earnings — with the resulting tax payable in two to eight installments, sharply reducing the cost of repatriating offshore profit stockpiles.
Proponents' stated rationale, reflected in the bill's title and sponsor's introductory remarks, is job creation and reform of a system that taxes foreign income of U.S. companies.

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury bears the cost of the near-exemption on foreign dividends and intangible income and the discounted transition tax, meaning the burden shifts to other taxpayers or to reduced federal revenue — partially offset by the bill's own anti-avoidance rules, which tax low-taxed foreign income currently, tighten the foreign tax credit, and accelerate worldwide interest allocation.

drawbacks.text: The bill's centerpiece is a very large permanent tax cut for multinational corporations: a 95% deduction on foreign dividends and a 50% deduction on foreign intangible income would leave the Treasury collecting only a small fraction of current tax on that income.

The discounted transition rule would let companies clear decades of accumulated offshore profits at roughly 30% of the normal rate, in up to eight installments, a concession to the largest holders of offshore cash.

The bill makes permanent the exceptions for active financing income and the look-through rule for controlled foreign corporations, locking in existing carve-outs that let banking, insurance, and holding-company structures avoid current U.S. tax.

A good-faith defense of the bill is that the current system taxes foreign profits twice and traps them offshore; but the bill's own offsetting provisions are narrow — taxing only foreign income taxed below half the U.S. corporate rate — and no official revenue estimate of the net cost appears in the record provided.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a genuine structural trade: it ends taxation of most repatriated foreign profits while adding anti-avoidance rules that raise tax on some offshore income. But the exemption side dwarfs the enforcement side — a 95% deduction on dividends, a 50% deduction on intangible income, and a 70% deduction on repatriated stockpiles — with no scoring in the record showing the anti-avoidance rules come close to paying for the cuts. The cost would fall on the general Treasury while the benefit goes to a specific set of very large corporations.

outcome.mechanism: Enzi introduced the bill alone and it sat in the Senate Finance Committee without a hearing, markup, or vote until the 112th Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on February 9, 2012, and its sponsor gave introductory remarks on the Senate floor the same day.
It was read twice and referred to the Senate Finance Committee on the day of introduction; the record shows no further action of any kind for the remainder of the 112th Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The pre-existing worldwide tax system stayed in place, so the federal Treasury kept collecting tax on foreign profits of U.S. corporations as before, and multinationals never received the exemptions. Taxpayers generally are better off than under the bill, while the concentrated interest it was written for gained nothing.

for.name: Sen. Michael B. Enzi
for.role: U.S. Senator from Wyoming and sole sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, gave introductory floor remarks, and saw it referred to the Finance Committee.

against.name: Max Baucus
against.what_they_did: Took no recorded action to schedule the bill for consideration during the two-year Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and no senator cosponsored the bill, so no partisan breakdown exists; the only recorded support was its lone Republican sponsor.

industries.note: The bill gives them a 95% deduction on dividends from foreign subsidiaries, a 50% deduction on foreign intangible income, and a discounted transition tax on repatriated earnings — a large net tax cut. It is partially offset by a new current tax on foreign income taxed below half the U.S. corporate rate and by repealing the foreign-base-company sales and services exclusions.

The 50% deduction on foreign intangible income specifically rewards companies whose patents and software are developed in the U.S. and licensed or sold abroad. The revenue given up is made up by other taxpayers.

industries.industry: U.S. companies holding large offshore profit stockpiles
industries.note: The transition election lets them repatriate accumulated pre-2013 earnings while deducting 70% of the amount and paying the rest in up to eight installments. Their gain comes directly out of federal revenue.

industries.industry: Offshore banking and insurance operations of U.S. financial firms
industries.note: The bill makes permanent the active financing income exception and the look-through rule, locking in carve-outs that shield foreign financing and insurance subsidiaries from current U.S. tax. These structures would remain the standing channel for shifting financial income offshore.
